title: Common Catabolic Pathways
objectives: Understand the structure and function of the Citric Acid Cycle (TCA/Krebs Cycle)
Describe the detailed enzymatic steps and regulation of the TCA cycle
Explain the flow of electrons through the Electron Transport Chain (ETC) and ATP synthesis
Analyze clinical disorders related to TCA cycle and oxidative phosphorylation

overview.title: Pathway Overview
overview.content:
The common catabolic pathways represent the final converging point of energy metabolism where carbohydrates, lipids, and proteins are broken down into their simplest forms and oxidized to generate energy. These pathways mainly include the Citric Acid Cycle (also called Krebs or TCA cycle) and Oxidative Phosphorylation (OXPHOS). They occur in the mitochondria of cells that possess this organelle and are essential for aerobic ATP production. The Citric Acid Cycle oxidizes Acetyl-CoA into CO2, while simultaneously reducing NAD+ and FAD to NADH and FADH2, which are then utilized in the electron transport chain to produce ATP. These pathways are tightly regulated and linked to both energy production and biosynthetic functions.

Biological Significance

  • Energy Production: They provide the majority of ATP needed for cellular functions under aerobic conditions.
  • Metabolic Integration: They serve as a hub where carbohydrates (via glycolysis), lipids (via β-oxidation), and amino acids (via transamination and deamination) converge as Acetyl-CoA.
  • Biosynthetic Precursors: Intermediates from the TCA cycle are siphoned off for the synthesis of amino acids, glucose (via gluconeogenesis), heme, and fatty acids.
  • Regulatory Node: These cycles respond to hormonal and allosteric signals to balance energy supply with cellular demand.

Key Inputs and Outputs

Inputs

  • Acetyl-CoA (from pyruvate, fatty acids, or amino acids)
  • 3 NAD+, 1 FAD
  • GDP (or ADP) and inorganic phosphate (Pi)
  • Oxygen (as the final electron acceptor)

Outputs

  • 3 NADH and 1 FADH2 (for OXPHOS)
  • 1 GTP (or ATP via substrate-level phosphorylation)
  • 2 CO2 molecules (by decarboxylation)
  • Oxaloacetate (regenerated to continue the cycle)

key_enzymes.title: Key Enzymes
key_enzymes.content:
Pyruvate Dehydrogenase Complex (PDHC)

Function: Converts pyruvate to acetyl-CoA; serves as a link between glycolysis and TCA

Subunits: E1 (pyruvate decarboxylase), E2 (dihydrolipoyl transacetylase), E3 (dihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase)

Cofactors: TPP (B1), Lipoate, FAD (B2), CoA (B5), NAD+ (B3)

Regulation: Inhibited by NADH, acetyl-CoA, and fatty acids; activated by CoA-SH, NAD+, and insulin (via phosphatase activity)

Clinical Relevance

Deficiency or inhibition (e.g. arsenic, thiamin deficiency) leads to accumulation of lactate and lactic acidosis.

Isocitrate Dehydrogenase

Reaction: Isocitrate → α-ketoglutarate + CO2 + NADH

Cofactor: NAD+, Mg2+

Regulation: Activated by ADP and Ca2+; inhibited by ATP and NADH

α-Ketoglutarate Dehydrogenase

Function: Converts α-ketoglutarate to succinyl-CoA; releases CO2 and produces NADH

Cofactors: Same as PDHC

Regulation: Inhibited by NADH, succinyl-CoA, arsenate; activated by Ca2+

regulation.title: Pathway Regulation
regulation.content:
TCA Regulation

Allosteric Control: High NADH and ATP inhibit key enzymes like citrate synthase, isocitrate dehydrogenase, and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase. ADP and Ca2+ serve as activators during energy demand.

Covalent Modification: PDHC is phosphorylated (inactivated) by its kinase in high-energy states and dephosphorylated (activated) by phosphatase, especially in response to insulin or Ca2+.

OXPHOS Regulation

Substrate Availability: Rate of oxidative phosphorylation is tightly coupled to availability of ADP (acceptor control).

Inhibitors: Rotenone (Complex I), Antimycin A (III), Cyanide and CO (IV), Oligomycin (ATP synthase)

Uncouplers: Agents like DNP dissipate the proton gradient, leading to heat production instead of ATP synthesis.

clinical.title: Clinical Notes
clinical.content:
Lactic Acidosis and PDHC Deficiency

Pathology: Inhibition of PDHC (due to thiamin deficiency or toxins) leads to pyruvate accumulation and increased lactate formation.

Symptoms: Neurological dysfunction, metabolic acidosis, especially in neonates

Diagnosis: Enzyme assays, lactate-to-pyruvate ratio, thiamin levels

Treatment: High-fat, low-carb diet, thiamin supplements

Mitochondrial Myopathies

Examples: MELAS syndrome, Fatal Infantile Myopathy

Cause: mtDNA mutations affecting ETC complexes I or IV

Symptoms: Muscle weakness, stroke-like episodes, lactic acidosis

Diagnosis: Muscle biopsy, mtDNA sequencing

faqs.title: FAQs
faqs.content:
What are the major outputs of the TCA cycle per acetyl-CoA?+
Three NADH, one FADH2, one GTP (equivalent to ATP), and two CO2.
How is ATP produced during OXPHOS?+
NADH and FADH2 donate electrons to the ETC, driving proton pumps that generate a gradient used by ATP synthase to produce ATP.
What is the effect of uncouplers on energy production?+
They allow proton flow without ATP synthesis, converting energy into heat—used physiologically in brown fat for thermogenesis.
What vitamins are essential for TCA and PDHC?+
Thiamin (B1), Riboflavin (B2), Niacin (B3), Pantothenic Acid (B5), and Lipoic Acid.
